title: For Your Eyes Is All My Heart Endures
intro: Al-Mutanabbi wrote this for Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid prince of Aleppo, when an envoy of the Byzantine emperor arrived with a letter asking for an exchange of prisoners; the commentator Ibn al-Iflili dates it to 341 AH (952 CE). It opens as a love poem: the beloved's eyes and what they have done to him, his restraint in love, the days of his youth, a parting one evening. A single comparison then carries it to the prince's spears and raids, to the emperor who comes asking like a beggar, and to his envoy, who walks up the carpet so dazzled that he cannot tell whether he is approaching a sea or climbing towards the moon. Then comes the poet's pride in his place at court, and a return to the prince, ending on the thought that merit wins nothing without fortune on its side. The opening line is famous, critics praised the turn from love to praise as one of the smoothest in Arabic, and the second half of line 37, “whoever jostles the sea will drown”, became a proverb.

translation: Your eyes cause all my heart meets and has met;
love owns what is gone of me, and what remains.
1.sharh: He blames her eyes for everything his heart has suffered and will suffer. Love has wasted his body: what is gone, love took, and what is left, love is still consuming.

translation: I was never one to let passion into his heart,
but whoever sees your eyelids falls in love.
2.sharh: He was never the kind of man who falls in love; the fault is in her eyes, which make a lover of anyone who sees them. Arabic poets speak of the eyelids, lashes and all, for the look of the eyes.

translation: Between favour and anger, nearness and distance,
there is room for tears that tremble in the eye.
3.sharh: A lover weeps whatever happens: when she is pleased with him or angry, near him or far. Every state gives his tears a reason to well up.

translation: Love is sweetest when the lover is unsure of union
and of parting, and hopes and fears all his life.
4.sharh: Love is sweetest while it is uncertain. Once a lover is sure of union the pleasure goes, and once he despairs he loses even the pleasure of hope. The commentator al-Wahidi lists earlier poets who said the same.

translation: Many a girl, cross out of coquetry, drunk with youth:
I sent the first bloom of my youth to plead with her.
5.sharh: The “and” that opens the line means “many a”. He recalls girls who played at being angry with him, sure of his love. His youth spoke for him, and they relented.

translation: Many a love with gleaming teeth, honey-sweet and bright:
I hid my mouth, and they kissed the crown of my head.
6.sharh: A beloved with white teeth and sweet breath moved to kiss him, and he covered his mouth out of restraint, so the kiss landed on his head. He boasts of loving without going beyond what is allowed.

translation: And necks of gazelles, like yours, came to visit me,
and I could not tell the bare from the necklaced.
7.sharh: Women with long, graceful necks like his beloved's came to see him, and he kept his eyes lowered so carefully that he never noticed which of them wore necklaces.

translation: Not every lover, alone with his love, holds back
as I do, and pleases her when horsemen clash.
8.sharh: Few lovers combine restraint in private with courage in war, and he claims both. The women of Arabia prized a man who could defend them when the horsemen met.

translation: May God water the days of youth with what delights them
and works like old Babylonian wine.
9.sharh: Praying for rain on a place or a time one loves is an old Arabic blessing. He asks that the days of youth be given what delights them and works like aged wine.

translation: When you wear time, taking your pleasure in it,
you are the one worn out; what you wore does not wear.
10.sharh: Time is a garment that never wears out; it is the one who wears it who does. People pass, and time stays new.

translation: I never saw the like of those glances the day they left:
they sent the cruellest death from hearts that wished us none.
11.sharh: On the day the women left they could only send glances, for fear of watchers. Those glances killed the men who received them, though they came from hearts that wished them no harm. Commentators argued over this line; this is the reading al-Wahidi preferred.

translation: They turned their eyes about, bewildered, as if
the pupils had been set on quicksilver.
12.sharh: Waiting for the moment of parting, the women's eyes could not rest anywhere. They darted about as if the pupils floated on mercury, which never stays still.

translation: That evening, weeping kept us from looking,
and the fear of parting from the sweetness of farewell.
13.sharh: Tears blurred their eyes so they could not see the ones who were leaving, and the dread of separation spoiled even the sweetness of saying goodbye. They could neither look nor take their leave.

translation: We bade them farewell, and parting was in us
like the spears of Ibn Abi al-Hayja' in an army's heart.
14.sharh: Parting cut through them as Sayf al-Dawla's spears cut through an army. This one comparison carries the poem from love to praise, a smooth turn that Arabic critics admired.

translation: Deadly, piercing spears: to them David's woven mail,
when they strike it, is like a spider's web.
15.sharh: The prince's spears kill and pierce. Coats of mail, which tradition credits to David, whom God taught to work iron, are no more to them than cobwebs.

translation: They lead the way to the kings of armies, as if
choosing and picking out the souls of champions.
16.sharh: The spears lead the men who carry them to the commanders of enemy armies, as if they singled out the souls of the bravest. Al-Wahidi reads it so; others say the spears find their own way to the commanders.

translation: They cleave every coat of mail and breastplate on them,
and cut through every wall and trench to them.
17.sharh: No armour keeps the enemy safe, and no fortress: the spears split the one and cut through the other.

translation: He raids with them from al-Luqan to Wasit,
and plants them between the Euphrates and Jilliq.
18.sharh: His raids reach from al-Luqan in Byzantine land to Wasit in Iraq, and when he makes camp he plants his spears anywhere from the Euphrates to Damascus. The line maps the range of his wars.

translation: He brings them back red, as if the unbroken ones
wept blood in pity for the shattered.
19.sharh: The spears come back red with enemy blood. The poet imagines the ones still whole weeping blood for those that broke.

translation: Do not tell him what I say, my friends: he
is so brave that talk of battle makes him long for it.
20.sharh: Arabic poets often speak to two companions. He asks them not to repeat this account of battle to the prince, who is so brave that hearing of war makes him long for it. Al-Wahidi traces the idea to the poet Kuthayyir.

translation: His fingers strike hard with the edges of swords,
and play with the edges of finely turned words.
21.sharh: The prince is a fighter and a master of words, at home with wordplay. The two halves mirror each other: hard-striking with the edges of swords, playful with the edges of speech.

translation: Asking him is like asking the rain for a drop;
blaming him is like telling the heavens to slow down.
22.sharh: Whoever asks him for anything, however much, asks too little, like a man asking the rain for one drop. Others read it as: he gives unasked, as rain falls. Blaming him for his generosity is as useless as telling the turning heavens to go gently.

translation: You gave until you had given to people of every faith,
and praise came to you in every tongue.
23.sharh: His gifts have reached people of every religion, and they thank him in every language.

translation: The Byzantine king saw how you delight in giving,
and stood where the fawning beggar stands.
24.sharh: Seeing how gladly the prince gives, the Byzantine emperor approached him like a flattering beggar. This is the letter the envoy brought, asking for an exchange of prisoners.

translation: He has abandoned his hard spears, humbled,
to one more practised and skilled at thrusting.
25.sharh: The emperor gave up the fight, not by choice, and left the spears to a better fighter, sending a letter instead. Samhari spears were famous for their hardness.

translation: He wrote to you from a land far out of reach,
yet near for the swift horses around you.
26.sharh: The emperor's land is far for anyone else, but close for the prince's swift horses.

translation: His envoy travelled the road your night raids took,
and walked on nothing but split skulls.
27.sharh: The envoy came by the same road the prince's raids had taken, and it was paved with the skulls of the Byzantine dead.

translation: When he drew near, his place was hidden from him
by the gleam of flashing, glittering steel.
28.sharh: Approaching the prince's court, the envoy was so dazzled by the glitter of weapons that he could no longer see where he was.

translation: He came forward on the carpet and could not tell
if he walked towards a sea or climbed to the moon.
29.sharh: Walking up the carpet, the envoy could not tell whether he was approaching a sea, for the prince's generosity, or climbing to the full moon, for his majesty. Some copies have “between the rows” of courtiers for “on the carpet”.

translation: Your enemies never turned you from their lives' blood
with anything like submission in polished words.
30.sharh: Nothing saves the prince's enemies from his sword except humility, such as a submissive letter in elegant language.

translation: Before this letter, when you wrote to him,
you wrote on the back of the Domesticus's head.
31.sharh: Until now the prince's letters to the emperor were written with the sword, on the head of the Byzantine commander: his wounds were the message.

translation: Grant him safe conduct, and he is a beggar asking;
give him the sword's edge, and how well he earned it.
32.sharh: If the prince grants safe conduct, it is because the emperor came asking, and he never turns a beggar away. If he gives him the sword, the emperor has earned it as an enemy at war.

translation: Did the gleaming, cutting swords leave any of them
a captive to ransom, or a slave to set free?
33.sharh: The prince's swords killed so many that they left no captive to ransom and no slave to free: a pointed remark when the envoy had come about an exchange of prisoners.

translation: They came to the swords' edges as sandgrouse come to water,
and passed over them rank after rank.
34.sharh: The enemy came to the swords as sandgrouse come to water, flock after flock from far away, and the swords took them rank after rank.

translation: Through Sayf al-Dawla, a light, I reached a rank
with which I stirred all between west and east.
35.sharh: Here the poet turns to himself. Serving Sayf al-Dawla, whose fame shines like light, has raised him to a rank known from west to east. The commentaries have “I lit up” (anartu) where the reciter says “I stirred” (athartu).

translation: When he wants to play with a fool's beard,
he shows him my dust and tells him, “Catch up.”
36.sharh: When the prince wants to make fun of a foolish rival poet, he points to the dust al-Mutanabbi has raised far ahead and tells the fool to catch up.

translation: The grief of the envious was never what I aimed at;
but whoever jostles the sea will drown.
37.sharh: He never set out to hurt his envious rivals; they suffer because they try to compete with him, like a man who wrestles the sea and drowns. The second half became a proverb.

translation: The prince tests people with his judgement,
and knowingly looks away from every charlatan.
38.sharh: The prince sees through everyone, and out of generosity he lets the frauds pass without exposing them.

translation: But lowering the eye's glance does no good
when the heart's eye is not lowered.
39.sharh: The fraud gains nothing from the prince's lowered eyes, because his heart still sees him. The Arabic plays on tarf, the glance, and itraq, lowering it.

translation: You who are hunted, be his neighbour, and be safe;
you who are deprived, go to him, and be provided for.
40.sharh: The prince is a refuge for the hunted and a provider for the poor.

translation: Most cowardly of horsemen, keep his company, and dare;
bravest of the brave, leave him, and fear.
41.sharh: His company makes cowards brave, from his example or from trust in his protection, and leaving him makes even the brave afraid. The Arabic plays on fariqhu, “leave him”, and tafraq, “you will fear”.

translation: When enemies work to bring down his glory,
his fortune works against their plots in fury.
42.sharh: When enemies plot against his glory, his good fortune turns their plots back on them. “Glory” and “fortune”, majd and jadd, are a play on sound.

translation: Plain merit wins no victory over enemies
unless it is the merit of one blessed with fortune.
43.sharh: Merit alone does not defeat enemies unless fortune goes with it, and the prince has both.

5.2.5.head: رَيِّق
5.2.5.meaning: Rayyiq: the first and best of anything; here, the first bloom of youth.

6.1.1.head: أَشنَب
6.1.1.meaning: Ashnab: having white, gleaming teeth, a beauty prized in a beloved.

6.2.5.head: مَفرِق
6.2.5.meaning: Mafriq: the parting of the hair, the crown of the head.

7.2.3.head: عاطِل
7.2.3.meaning: Atil: a woman wearing no jewellery.

9.2.3.head: البابِلِيّ
9.2.3.meaning: Babylonian: wine from Babil in Iraq, famous for its wine.

14.2.2-4.meaning: The son of Abu al-Hayja': Sayf al-Dawla, whose father was Abu al-Hayja' Abdallah ibn Hamdan. Hayja' means battle.

15.1.3-4.meaning: “David's weaving”: mail armour. The Quran says God made iron soft for David, and he made coats of mail.

16.2.3.head: الكُماة
16.2.3.meaning: Kumat: champions, men hidden in their armour.

18.1.4.head: اللُّقان
18.1.4.meaning: Al-Luqan: a place in Byzantine territory.

18.1.5.head: واسِط
18.1.5.meaning: Wasit: a city in Iraq between Basra and Kufa, founded by al-Hajjaj.

18.2.1.head: رَكَزَ
18.2.1.meaning: Plants a spear in the ground, as when making camp: rakaza, yarkuzu or yarkizu. The reciter says yurkizu, a form the dictionaries do not give in this sense.

18.2.4.head: جِلِّق
18.2.4.meaning: Jilliq: an old name for Damascus and its countryside.

22.2.4.head: الفَلَك
22.2.4.meaning: Falak: the sphere of the heavens, thought to carry the stars round on a course that never changes.

25.1.3.head: السَّمهَرِيّ
25.1.3.meaning: Samhari: hard, straight spears, said to be named after Samhar, a man who straightened spear shafts.

29.2.3.meaning: He walks. Al-Wahidi has yas'a, “he hastens”.

31.2.4.head: القَذال
31.2.4.meaning: Qadhal: the back of the head, the nape.

31.2.5.head: الدُّمُستُق
31.2.5.meaning: Dumustuq: the Domesticus, commander of the Byzantine army, from the Greek domestikos.

32.1.3-4.meaning: “Safe conduct from you”. The commentaries have “some safe conduct” (ba'd al-aman).

33.1.3-4.meaning: “The white, the cutting”: swords, called white for their gleam.

33.2.1.meaning: A captive. Al-Wahidi has habis, “one held prisoner”.

34.1.3-4.meaning: As sandgrouse come to water: they fly long distances to drink and arrive flock after flock.

34.2.3-5.meaning: Rank after rank: razdaq, a Persian word for a row, as al-Wahidi and al-Ma'arri have it. The reciter says zardaq, with the first two letters swapped.

35.2.1.meaning: I stirred up, as dust is stirred. The commentaries have anartu, “I lit up”.

36.1.4-5.meaning: “Play with his beard”: make a fool of him.

38.2.5.head: المُمَخرِق
38.2.5.meaning: Mumakhriq: a charlatan, a dealer in tricks; al-Wahidi calls it an Iraqi word.
